陈养山.cast: The book's subject; a Central Special Branch intelligence officer, born Cheng Yangshan in Shangyu, Zhejiang, 1906.
陈养山.note: Original name 程仰山 Cheng Yangshan; changed to 陈养山 on taking up secret work.

恽代英.cast: CCP youth organizer and editor of China Youth; the man who drew Chen Yangshan to revolution. 1895-1931.

贺龙.cast: Nanchang Uprising commander whom Chen Yangshan shielded in Shanghai in 1927; later a PLA marshal.

章素贞.note: Chen Yangshan's wife; later joined the Central Special Branch.

陈赓.note: Ran the Central Special Branch's operations; recruited Zhang Suzhen.

顾顺章.note: authority.json: agreed 'Gu Shunzhang'. His 1931 defection gutted the CCP underground.

中央特科.note: authority.json: agreed 'the Central Special Branch' / 'Central Special Branch'. The CCP Central Committee's clandestine intelligence and security organ, Shanghai, from 1927.

中国青年.note: The Socialist Youth League's magazine, edited by Yun Daiying.

工部局.note: The Shanghai Municipal Council, governing body of the International Settlement.

ch01.note: A Chinese man of this milieu carried several names: a given name (here 仰山 Yangshan) and a formal zi or courtesy name (应骝 Yingliu) taken at adulthood and used by peers. Chen also changed his surname from Cheng (程) to Chen (陈) when he entered underground work, a common precaution; the book's title and this translation use the revolutionary name throughout.

The jinshi, the highest degree in the imperial civil-service examinations and the gateway to senior office. A salt commissioner (盐政使) oversaw the lucrative state salt monopoly; the grandfather's rank marks the family as one of real standing before its decline.

The Shuijing zhu, a celebrated early-sixth-century work by Li Daoyuan expanding a terse older gazetteer of China's rivers into a vast topographical and folkloric survey. Citing it lends the local lake an ancient pedigree.

A classic tale of filial devotion. The historical Cao E stele (曹娥碑) is real and famous, chiefly for a riddling inscription later added to it; the drowning legend is traditional rather than documented. Cao'e, the girl's name, was in time given to the river and the county town themselves.

Shiye jiuguo, the early-twentieth-century conviction that China could be saved by building modern commerce and industry rather than by politics. Chen's abandonment of it for revolution is the arc of this chapter; the parallel slogan 'salvation through education' appears below.

ch01.anchor: the May Fourth Movement broke out in 1919
ch01.note: The student-led protests of May 4, 1919, against the Versailles award of German concessions in Shandong to Japan, which swelled into a nationwide movement for cultural renewal and against imperialism and warlordism. It is conventionally taken as the seedbed of Chinese Communism.

The Erqi incident of February 7, 1923: the warlord Wu Peifu, of the Zhili clique that then controlled the Beijing-Hankou line, crushed the railwaymen's strike by force. It became a founding martyrdom of the Chinese labor movement. The casualty figures here are the book's.

ch01.anchor: more than two thousand li of it
ch01.note: The li is a traditional Chinese unit of distance, in the modern period standardized at half a kilometer; two thousand li is roughly a thousand kilometers, about the length of the Beijing-Hankou line.
Zhongguo qingnian, launched in 1923 as the organ of the Socialist Youth League and edited by Yun Daiying, among the most influential progressive periodicals of its day among young readers.

ch01.anchor: the Socialist Youth League of China
ch01.note: The Communist Party's youth organization, founded 1922, from which promising members like Chen graduated into full Party membership; the forerunner of today's Communist Youth League.

ch01.anchor: the League Central secretary, Ren Bishi
ch01.note: Ren Bishi (1904-1950), then a very young secretary of the Youth League's central committee, later one of the five top leaders of the CCP alongside Mao, Liu Shaoqi, Zhou Enlai and Zhu De.
Lenin died on January 21, 1924; memorial issues of the Chinese left press introduced many young readers, Chen among them, to the Soviet model as a template for China's own revolution.

The closing image of Yun Daiying's prison poem. 'A captive of Chu' (Chu qiu) is a classical byword, from the Zuo zhuan, for a prisoner who keeps his dignity and loyalty in captivity. The book reproduces the poem in Zhou Enlai's own 1953 hand and prints it as shown here; other published texts of the poem read slightly differently in two characters, a variation left as the book gives it.

The nationwide anti-imperialist upheaval of 1925, touched off by the events this section narrates: British-officered police in Shanghai's foreign settlement shooting Chinese demonstrators. It marks the high tide of the mid-1920s revolution.

The foreign-run enclave in central Shanghai, outside Chinese jurisdiction, administered by the Shanghai Municipal Council (the 工部局) with its own police force and, for cases involving Chinese, the Mixed Court. That an armed foreign administration policed Chinese streets is the standing grievance behind this whole episode.

K. J. McEuen, Commissioner of the Shanghai Municipal Police in 1925. His order to fire and the killings that followed on Nanjing Road on May 30 made him a lasting symbol of the settlement's use of force against Chinese; he was later removed amid the outcry.

ch01.anchor: carried the Northern Expedition victoriously into Hubei
ch01.note: The Northern Expedition (1926-1928), the Kuomintang-Communist military campaign out of Guangdong to defeat the northern warlords and reunify China; its early advance into the central provinces frames much of this chapter's action.

On April 12, 1927, Chiang Kai-shek turned on his Communist allies in Shanghai, massacring Communists and labor activists with gangster help and ending the first Kuomintang-Communist united front. The 'white terror' (白色恐怖) that follows in the book is the term for the wave of arrests and killings across the country afterward.

The Nanchang Uprising of August 1, 1927, the Communists' first armed revolt against the Kuomintang after the split; its date is now marked as the founding day of the People's Liberation Army. He Long, then a Kuomintang general, was one of its commanders, which is why he was hunted afterward.
The silver dollar (dayang) was the standard hard currency of Republican China; a hundred thousand of them was an enormous bounty, a measure of how badly the Kuomintang wanted He Long.

ch01.anchor: societies and secret sects of men like Huang Jinrong and Du Yuesheng
ch01.note: Huang Jinrong and Du Yuesheng were the bosses of Shanghai's Green Gang, the criminal fraternity that ran the city's underworld and that Chiang Kai-shek used as muscle in the April 12 purge; secret sects (会道门) were popular quasi-religious brotherhoods.

ch01.anchor: working in the Central Special Branch
ch01.note: The Zhongyang teke, the CCP's clandestine intelligence and security service in Shanghai, set up under Zhou Enlai after the 1927 split to protect the underground, gather intelligence, and punish traitors. It is the world in which the rest of this book unfolds, and Chen Yangshan's life's work.

Gu Shunzhang, a senior Special Branch operative whose capture and defection in April 1931 exposed much of the CCP underground and led directly to the deaths of many, including Yun Daiying. His name recurs through this book as its great catastrophe.
